title: K Values Nearest to a Target
statement:
You get a sorted array arr, a count k and a number x (which may or may not be in the array). Return the k elements of arr closest to x, in ascending order.

Element a is closer than b when |a − x| < |b − x|. On a tie in distance, the smaller value wins.

examples.why: 4 and 6 are both 1 away. The tie goes to the smaller value.
4 and 8 are 2 away, then 3 is 3 away and 10 is 4 away. The answer is printed sorted, not in order of distance.
x is below every element, so the closest ones are the first k.

constraints: arr is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: The answer is always a contiguous block of k elements in arr. Why?
So you only need the block's left edge, somewhere in 0..n − k. Compare the block starting at i with the one starting at i + 1: they differ only in arr[i] versus arr[i + k].
Binary search that left edge: if x − arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] − x, arr[mid] is strictly worse than arr[mid + k], so the window must start after mid. Otherwise it starts at mid or earlier.

explain.intuition:
In a sorted array, the k closest values to x always form one contiguous block: if you take some value, every value between it and x is at least as close. So the question becomes "where does the block start?", a single number between 0 and n − k.

Compare two neighbouring windows, one starting at mid and one at mid + 1. They share everything except arr[mid] (only in the first) and arr[mid + k] (only in the second). If arr[mid] is farther from x than arr[mid + k], shifting right is an improvement, and so is every shift up to the true start. Otherwise, the start is at mid or to its left. That one comparison is monotone, so you can binary-search it.
steps: Set lo = 0 and hi = n − k: the possible window starts.
If x − arr[mid] > arr[mid + k] − x, set lo = mid + 1; otherwise set hi = mid.
pitfalls: Comparing absolute values, |x − arr[mid]| > |arr[mid + k] − x|. With duplicates and x outside the window this can point the wrong way; the signed form is what makes the test monotone.
Breaking ties toward the larger value. Using ≥ instead of > shifts the window right on a tie.
Returning the elements in order of distance instead of sorted order.

solutions.title: Sort by distance
solutions.idea: Sort a copy by (distance, value), take the first k, and sort those back into ascending order.

solutions.title: Shrink from both ends
solutions.idea: Start with the whole array and drop the worse end until k elements remain. Ties drop the right end.

solutions.title: Binary search the window start
solutions.idea: The window start is monotone: move right exactly when arr[mid] is strictly farther than arr[mid + k].

followups: The values arrive unsorted. What is the best you can do then? (Think heap or quickselect.)
Answer many queries with different x on the same array. What changes?
